hero.name: Sapna
hero.who: a 34-year-old primary school teacher in Lucknow trying to win support for a reading corner

story.b: Sapna teaches Class 3 at a school in Aliganj, Lucknow. For months she has dreamed of a reading corner in her classroom: a small shelf, a mat and fifty storybooks in Hindi and English. She has prepared a neat page with costs. On Wednesday she catches the principal, Mrs Khanna, in the corridor during exam week, just after a parent has complained loudly about seating. Sapna gives her well-practised speech. Mrs Khanna barely listens and says there is no money this year. Sapna goes back to the staffroom feeling foolish. The idea was good. The page was clear. She cannot understand why it fell so flat, when a colleague got new sports equipment approved last month.

ask.q: Sapna's well-prepared request was rejected in a busy corridor during exam week. What did she most likely overlook?
o: Her proposal was not detailed enough
The moment and the mood just before she asked
Mrs Khanna simply does not like reading programmes
ask.why: The same request can land very differently depending on what just happened. Mrs Khanna was stressed and distracted, so even a good idea had little chance. More detail would not fix the timing, and assuming dislike stops Sapna from trying again at a better moment.

chapters.take: What happens just before you ask can matter as much as what you ask.

story.b: Sapna decides not to try again in a rush. She watches for a better moment. Two weeks later, the school's Class 3 children win first prize in a district storytelling contest, and Mrs Khanna announces it proudly at assembly. That afternoon the principal is in her office, smiling, with a box of laddoos on her desk for the staff. Sapna knocks, congratulates her and mentions that the winning children are the ones who read the most at home. Then she gently brings out her one-page plan. Mrs Khanna reads it properly this time. She does not say yes at once, but she asks Sapna for the list of books and a quote from the bookshop in Aminabad.

ask.q: Sapna wants to raise the reading corner again. When should she ask?
o: Right now by message, before she loses courage
During the next busy staff meeting, so others can hear
In a calm, positive moment, like right after the school's good news
ask.why: People are more open just after a good result, when they feel relaxed and proud. Asking then gives the idea a fair hearing. A rushed message or a crowded meeting brings back the same distraction that sank her first attempt.

chapters.take: Choose your moment. People hear ideas better when they feel calm and proud.

story.h: The notice board by the gate
story.b: At the parent-teacher meeting, Sapna notices something. Almost every parent asks about marks and tuition, and nobody asks about reading. Then she looks at the notice board by the gate. It shows only the toppers' photos and exam dates. That is what parents see every single morning, so that is what feels important. Sapna realises attention is shaping their worries. With the principal's permission, she puts up a small new board beside it, called Books We Loved This Month, with children's drawings of their favourite stories. Within a week, parents waiting at pickup time stand and read it. One father asks her where he can buy the book about the clever crow.

ask.q: Parents only ask Sapna about marks. What is the most effective way to make reading feel important to them?
o: Put reading where their attention already goes, like a display at the gate
Lecture parents about reading at the next meeting
Send a long circular that most parents will skim
ask.why: What people keep seeing starts to feel important. A display where parents wait every day quietly raises reading in their minds. A lecture can make people defensive, and a long circular rarely gets enough attention to change what feels important.

chapters.take: What people keep seeing starts to feel important. Notice who is steering attention.

story.b: Sapna needs parent volunteers to read to the children on Saturday mornings. Last year a similar request got two names. This time, at the start of the parents' meeting, she does not begin with the request. She asks a question first: what is the first story you remember loving as a child? The room changes. A mother talks about her grandmother's ghost stories in Awadhi. A father who drives an e-rickshaw remembers a comic he read under a blanket. People are laughing and nodding. Only then does Sapna explain the Saturday reading plan and pass around a sheet. When the meeting ends, it has eleven names, and the e-rickshaw driver has offered to read twice.

ask.q: Sapna wants parent volunteers. How should she open the meeting?
o: Start with how few parents helped last year, to make them feel guilty
Start with a question that brings back their own love of stories
Start straight with the sign-up sheet to save time
ask.why: An opener puts people in a frame of mind before the real request arrives. Remembering their own childhood stories helps parents feel the value of reading, so saying yes comes naturally. Guilt makes people defensive, and jumping to the sheet skips the moment that warms them up.

chapters.take: The question you ask first shapes the answer you get next.

story.b: Sapna has a small book budget approved, and on Sunday she visits a big new bookstore in a mall in Gomti Nagar. Soft music plays. The lights are warm. The children's section smells of new paper and coffee from the cafe next door. Without meaning to, she finds herself holding a beautiful imported box set that costs half her budget. She pauses and looks around. The music, the lights and the cosy chairs are all quietly working on her. She puts the set back, checks her list, and buys most books from the old shop in Aminabad instead. But she takes one lesson home. For her reading corner, she buys a soft rug, cushions and a string of fairy lights.

ask.q: In the cosy bookstore, Sapna feels drawn to a costly box set. What should she do?
o: Notice how the setting is nudging her and check against her list first
Buy it, since feeling good about it means it is the right choice
Leave the store at once and never shop in malls again
ask.why: Music, light and comfort shape feelings without our noticing, and those feelings can steer spending. Pausing to see the cues and checking her list keeps the choice her own. Trusting the warm feeling lets the setting decide, and avoiding all malls is an overreaction.

chapters.take: Settings work quietly on our choices. Notice them before you decide.

story.b: Sapna learns that the owner of the old Aminabad bookshop studied at her school decades ago. When she places her order, she mentions it honestly, and his face lights up. He gives the school a generous discount and adds five books free, for his old school, he says. A week later, a stranger messages Sapna on WhatsApp. He says he is also a teacher from Lucknow, a fellow educator who understands her struggles, and he wants her to buy an expensive online certificate course. Sapna feels the same warm pull of being one of us. She notices it, smiles, and decides to look into the course carefully before replying.

ask.q: A stranger calling himself a fellow Lucknow teacher pushes Sapna to buy a costly course. What should she do?
o: Trust him, since teachers always look out for each other
Block him at once, since anyone using shared identity must be a cheat
Notice the pull of shared identity and judge the course on its own merits
ask.why: Feeling part of the same group makes us say yes faster, which is why it is powerful and why it can be misused. Judging the course on its merits protects her. Blind trust lets the shared label think for her, and assuming every such message is a cheat is unfair, since she used shared roots honestly herself.

chapters.take: We say yes faster to one of us. Use that honestly and watch for it.

story.b: By the end of term, the reading corner in Class 3 is the busiest spot in the school. Fairy lights glow over a rug, and the shelf holds over sixty books. Every Saturday a parent volunteer reads aloud, and the e-rickshaw driver has become the children's favourite, doing all the voices. The Books We Loved board by the gate now has a waiting list for drawings. Mrs Khanna has asked Sapna to help set up a corner in Class 4 as well. Sapna still prepares her plans carefully, but now she also thinks about when she will ask, what she will say first and how the room will feel. She notices the same things when others ask her.

chapters.take: Good ideas need good moments. Prepare the mind before you make the ask.
